documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT VISIT

CC: Establishing care. Diabetes.

HPI: 57 y/o man here to set up primary care. Type 2 diabetes for roughly 14 years, diagnosed by his old PCP on routine labs. Has only ever been on metformin, now 1000 mg twice a day with meals, no GI trouble with it. Checks sugars rarely, "once a week if that." No lows. No polyuria/polydipsia. Atorvastatin 20 for cholesterol, takes it at night. Has never been on a blood pressure medicine and does not remember being told his pressure was high. Denies chest pain, dyspnea on exertion, calf pain with walking, foot numbness, blurry vision. Last eye exam he thinks was 3-4 years ago.

PMH: T2DM (~2005). Hyperlipidemia.
PSH: none.
Meds: metformin 1000 mg BID, atorvastatin 20 mg qhs. No OTCs or supplements.
Allergies: none known.
FH: Father had an MI at 65. Mother has type 2 diabetes. One sibling with high blood pressure.
SH: Office administrator, desk job. Never smoked. Does not drink. Walks some on weekends.

ROS: otherwise negative as above. PHQ-2 0.

Exam:
BP 159/99 (repeat by me after 5 min seated, similar). HR 63. Wt 104.2 kg, BMI 32.6.
Well-appearing, conversational.
Fundi: no AV nicking or hemorrhages on undilated look.
Neck: no JVD, no thyromegaly.
Chest clear to auscultation. Cardiac: regular, normal S1/S2, no gallop or murmur.
Abdomen: obese, soft, nontender.
Extremities: no ankle swelling.
Feet: skin intact, no calluses of note, nails ok. 10-g monofilament felt at all sites both feet. DP and PT pulses 2+ bilaterally.

A/P:
1. Type 2 diabetes - long duration, on metformin alone. A1c, CMP, urine albumin/creatinine today. Diabetic eye exam referral to optometry. Foot exam normal today.
2. Elevated blood pressure, no prior diagnosis - one office reading is not enough. Nurse BP check in about 3 weeks; asked him to bring a home cuff if he buys one.
3. Hyperlipidemia - continue atorvastatin 20. Lipid panel today.
4. Obesity - BMI over 30. Talked about portions and walking more on weekdays. He is interested.
5. Health maintenance - no colonoscopy on record, referred to GI for screening. Tdap today (no record of a tetanus shot). HCV and HIV screening once, ordered. Flu, pneumococcal and shingles vaccines in the fall.

RTC 3 months, sooner for the BP check.

documents.title: Your lab results from 3/12
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hi Gary,

Your labs from Tuesday are back.

- A1c 7.6%. That is a reasonable number after this many years of diabetes; our goal is to keep it at or under 7 to 7.5 for you.
- Kidney function (creatinine/eGFR) normal. Potassium and liver tests normal.
- Cholesterol: LDL 98, triglycerides 240. Keep the atorvastatin going.
- Urine albumin 47. This is a bit above normal (under 30). One reading can be high for ordinary reasons, so I'd like to repeat it at your June visit before we call it anything.
- Blood count normal. Hepatitis C and HIV screens negative.

See you for the blood pressure check in a few weeks.

Your primary care team

documents.title: Follow-up: diabetes, BP
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: 3-mo f/u. Feels fine. Bought a cuff two weeks ago, readings at home "about the same as here." Walking at lunch 2-3 days/wk. Taking metformin and atorvastatin daily. No headaches, CP, SOB. Colonoscopy in May was normal.

O: BP 155/95, HR 73, wt 102.4 kg.
Comfortable. Lungs clear. Heart: regular, no murmur or gallop. No pedal edema.

Labs today: A1c and repeat urine albumin/creatinine drawn, results to follow.

A/P:
# Hypertension, stage 2 - third elevated office set plus similar home numbers. Diagnosing essential hypertension. Discussed starting a medication today. He would rather try diet and walking first and "not add another pill yet." Reasonable for a short trial: less salt, more walking, home log. Recheck at next visit; if still up we start a drug.
# Albuminuria - March UACR 47; repeat pending today. If still >30 with normal eGFR, this meets CKD stage 1 from diabetes.
# T2DM - A1c pending. Continue metformin. Eye exam not yet scheduled, number given again.
# Hyperlipidemia - continue atorvastatin 20.

RTC 3-4 months. Flu/pneumonia/shingles shots in the fall.

Addendum 6/21: Repeat UACR 47 with eGFR 103. Two values over 30 three months apart. Adding CKD stage 1 (diabetic kidney disease) to problem list; diabetes recoded.

documents.title: June labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Gary - A1c 7.6%, steady. Kidney filtration is normal, but the urine protein (albumin) test was high again at 47. Two high readings three months apart means the diabetes is starting to affect the kidneys at an early stage, what we call stage 1 kidney disease. Blood pressure and sugar control are what protect the kidneys, so the home BP log matters. We'll go over it in the fall. Call with questions.

documents.title: Follow-up: hypertension
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Chief complaint: BP follow-up. Some headaches.

HPI: Here for hypertension f/u after the fall trial of diet and walking. Over the past month he has had occasional headaches, maybe 1-2 a week, dull, frontal, gone by evening on their own. None wake him from sleep, no vision change, no weakness or numbness, no worst-headache-of-life. Denies chest pain, SOB, orthopnea, leg swelling. Admits the home cuff has been in the closet since the summer; the few readings he did take at the pharmacy machine were "normal, in the 130s." Feels he gets keyed up at medical offices.

Meds: metformin 1000 BID, atorvastatin 20 daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
SH: never smoker, no alcohol, office administrator.

Exam: BP 158/96. Ht 178 cm, wt 101.4 kg, BMI 32.
NAD. Fundi without hypertensive changes (no AV nicking, hemorrhages or exudates). No JVD. Lungs clear, no crackles. Heart regular, no S3/S4 or murmur. No peripheral edema.

Labs today (fasting): creatinine 1.0, BUN 14, glucose 146. Lipids TC 190, HDL 40, LDL 100, TG 250. Urinalysis negative for protein and blood. A1c and UACR pending.

Assessment/plan:
1. Stage 2 essential hypertension, office readings consistently high; white-coat component suspected given his account of lower readings outside the office. Before committing him to a drug I want real numbers: home BP log twice daily (AM before meds, PM), seated, 2 readings each time, for 2-3 weeks, upload or bring in. No medication change today. Low-salt handout given. If home average is above 130/80 we start treatment.
2. Headaches - mild, no red flags on history or exam, no retinopathy. Possibly BP-related. Avoid daily NSAIDs given kidneys. Call if pattern changes.
3. T2DM with CKD stage 1 - fasting glucose 146; A1c and UACR pending. Creatinine 1.0 today, eGFR a little lower than last year's draws; likely day-to-day variation, recheck with the next BMP.
4. Hyperlipidemia - on atorvastatin 20, results reviewed above.
5. Obesity - BMI 32, weight down a little since spring. Encouraged.

RTC 3 months with log.

documents.title: Results from Monday
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hi Gary,

All your results from Monday are in.
- A1c 7.6%.
- Kidney: creatinine 1.0, eGFR 87, a little lower than last year; we'll recheck it with your next blood test. Urine albumin 46, still mildly elevated, about where it was. The routine urinalysis showed no protein or blood (that dipstick test isn't sensitive enough to pick up this small amount, which is why we do the albumin test).
- Cholesterol: LDL 100, HDL 40, triglycerides 250. Triglycerides run high with diabetes and extra weight; fewer sweets and refined carbs help.

The main job before April is the blood pressure log. Twice a day, two readings each time. You can type them into a portal message or bring the sheet.

Take care

documents.title: Follow-up: HTN, home BP log
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Visit in person, both masked. Door screen negative.

S: Three months since January. Taking metformin and atorvastatin every day. No complaints today; headaches have tapered off. Has been eating at home much more since the shutdown and walking the neighborhood most evenings, down about 3 kg.
Brought a printed home log, 23 days, mostly AM plus about half the evenings. I averaged it with him: most mornings run above 130/80, and the overall average is above goal even with the lower evening numbers. Office reading today is lower than his home average, which argues against white coat explaining this.

He also asked about aspirin. A coworker takes one and he wondered if he should, given diabetes and his father's heart attack.

O: BP 132/84. Wt 98.2 kg, BMI 31. Lungs clear, heart regular, no edema.

A/P:
# Essential hypertension with diabetic CKD stage 1 - home average above goal. Starting lisinopril 20 mg daily: lowers BP and also treats the albuminuria. Reviewed side effects: dry cough, dizziness, rare lip/tongue swelling (stop and call 911). BMP in 2 weeks for potassium and creatinine. Keep logging.
# Aspirin for primary prevention - went through it with him: diabetes, age and family history put him at higher risk, but for someone without known heart disease the benefit is small. That small benefit has to be weighed against a real chance of stomach or other bleeding. He understands it is a judgment call and wants to take it. Aspirin 81 mg daily, with food. Report black stools or easy bruising.
# T2DM, hyperlipidemia - no change. A1c next visit.

RTC 3 months, sooner by portal if BP log high or cough.

documents.title: Dry cough
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hello, I have had a dry tickly cough for about a week and a half now. No fever, I feel fine otherwise. Went to the walk-in on Tuesday because of everything going on and they did an x-ray which they said was normal and no covid test needed since no fever. My coworker said her blood pressure pill gave her a cough. Could that be the lisinopril? It's driving me nuts at night. Gary

documents.title: RE: Dry cough
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Gary, it very well could be. A dry cough is the most common side effect of lisinopril and it can start weeks after the first dose. I saw the x-ray report, it's normal. Let's see you Tuesday 6/9 to look you over and most likely switch you to a different BP medicine. Keep taking it until then unless you have any swelling of the lips or tongue (that would be call 911). If you get fever or shortness of breath, call us the same day.

documents.title: Acute: cough on ACE inhibitor
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Masked visit, screening negative at entry.

CC: dry cough x 2 weeks.

HPI: Started lisinopril 20 mg on 4/14. About 6 weeks later began a dry, nonproductive cough, worse lying down at night and with talking. No fever, chills, sputum, dyspnea or wheeze. No sick contacts, no nasal congestion or postnasal drip, no heartburn. Never smoker. Seen at urgent care 6/2: chest x-ray normal (report reviewed). Has kept taking the lisinopril. BP log on it has been better, mostly at or near goal.

Exam: BP 138/84, SpO2 98% RA. Afebrile by door screen. Talks in full sentences, occasional dry cough in room. Oropharynx clear. Lungs: good air movement, clear throughout, no wheeze or crackles. Heart regular.

A/P:
1. Cough due to ACE inhibitor - classic timing and character, normal x-ray, clear lungs, no infectious features. Stop lisinopril. Recording ACE inhibitor intolerance (cough) in allergies so no ACE inhibitor is restarted. Cough can take 1-4 weeks to settle after stopping.
2. Hypertension - starting amlodipine 5 mg daily in place of lisinopril. Can cause ankle swelling; let me know. Continue home log; message me readings in 2-3 weeks.
3. T2DM/CKD 1, hyperlipidemia - unchanged, labs at next routine visit.

RTC as scheduled in September; portal check-in in 3 weeks.

documents.title: RE: Update - cough and BP

documents.body: That's what I hoped to hear. Stay on amlodipine 5. I'll see you in September; we'll check sugar and kidney numbers then.

documents.title: Endocrinology consultation (visit 07/21/2021)
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
ENDOCRINOLOGY AND DIABETES CENTER
Consultation letter

Date of visit: 07/21/2021
Patient: Gary Kowalczyk, DOB 05/11/1961
Reason for referral: type 2 diabetes, worsening control on metformin

Dear Colleague,

Thank you for asking us to see Mr. Kowalczyk, a 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes of about 16 years' duration, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and early diabetic kidney disease.

History: He has been treated with metformin alone since diagnosis. He acknowledges his diet has been irregular this past year. On questioning he reports that for the past few months both feet have felt numb, "like they're half asleep," mostly at the toes and soles. He denies pain, burning or tingling. No foot ulcers. No claudication.

Current medications (per patient list): metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily.
Allergies: ACE inhibitors (cough).
Social: never smoker, no alcohol.

Examination: Vital signs within normal limits. Feet: dry skin bilaterally with calluses over the metatarsal heads. Vibration sense decreased in both feet. Monofilament: reduced sensation at multiple sites on both feet. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable but diminished bilaterally. No ulceration or deformity.

Laboratory (drawn in our lab this visit):
  Hemoglobin A1c 8.2%
  Fasting glucose 172 mg/dL
  Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL
  Total cholesterol 210 mg/dL
  LDL cholesterol 130 mg/dL
  HDL cholesterol 40 mg/dL
  Triglycerides 250 mg/dL

Assessment:
1. Type 2 diabetes mellitus, suboptimally controlled.
2. Diabetic peripheral neuropathy, both feet, with loss of protective sensation.
3. Diminished pedal pulses - consider vascular assessment.

Recommendations:
- Structured dietary change with a focus on carbohydrate portions and gradual weight loss; referral information for nutrition counseling provided.
- Continue metformin 1000 mg twice daily. No additional agent at this time; he is motivated to work on diet and weight first. We would reconsider if A1c is not improving in 3-6 months.
- Daily foot inspection, moisturize dry skin, well-fitting shoes, no barefoot walking.
- Suggest ankle-brachial index given the diminished pulses.

We are happy to see him again as needed.

Sincerely,
Endocrinology

CARDIOVASCULAR ASSOCIATES - CONSULTATION
Date: 07/26/2023
Patient: Gary Kowalczyk, 62-year-old man
Referring: primary care
Reason: exertional chest discomfort

History of present illness: Four months of central chest pressure, tight in quality, brought on by climbing stairs or walking uphill and relieved by rest within minutes. No rest pain, palpitations or syncope. Background of type 2 diabetes with neuropathy, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and peripheral arterial disease, all treated.

Medications (patient-provided list): metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily.
Allergies: ACE inhibitors (cough).
Social: does not smoke or drink alcohol.
Family history: father with myocardial infarction at 65.

Examination: BP 132/78, pulse 72/min, BMI 27. Comfortable. JVP not raised. Heart sounds normal, no murmur. Lungs clear. No peripheral edema.

Investigations today:
- Resting 12-lead ECG: normal.
- High-sensitivity troponin: within normal limits.
- Treadmill exercise test: positive for exercise-induced ST depression; no arrhythmia.

Impression: Stable angina pectoris. Symptoms are predictable, exertional and unchanged in pattern; no features of an acute coronary syndrome.

Plan:
- Medical management. Continue aspirin 81 mg and atorvastatin; continue current blood pressure treatment.
- Risk factor control with primary care: blood pressure, diabetes, lipids, activity within symptom limits.
- Return to clinic in 12 months, sooner for any change in pattern, rest pain or prolonged episodes; call 911 for pain lasting over 15 minutes.

Thank you for this referral.
Cardiology

documents.title: Cardiology follow-up (visit 07/17/2024)
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
CARDIOVASCULAR ASSOCIATES - FOLLOW-UP
Date of visit: 07/17/2024
Patient: Gary Kowalczyk, 63 y/o M
Diagnosis: stable angina pectoris

Interval history: Returns one year after his initial evaluation. Continues to have dull, central pressure-like chest discomfort after climbing stairs, resolving within a few minutes of rest. No rest pain, no nocturnal episodes, no syncope.

Medications (patient list): amlodipine, atorvastatin, metformin; lisinopril 20 mg daily; aspirin 81 mg daily. Also sildenafil as needed (urology).
Social: no tobacco or alcohol.

Exam: BP 138/84, heart rate 72/min. Cardiopulmonary exam normal.

Studies:
- ECG: nonspecific ST-T changes.
- Exercise stress test: positive for inducible ischemia.

Assessment: Stable angina with persistent exertional symptoms.

Plan:
1. Start sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg: one tablet under the tongue at the onset of chest discomfort; sit down after taking it, as it can drop blood pressure and cause lightheadedness. May repeat every 5 minutes up to 3 doses; call 911 if the discomfort is not improved 5 minutes after the first dose.
2. IMPORTANT: Never take nitroglycerin within 24 hours of sildenafil (or any erectile dysfunction medication of that class). The combination can cause a severe drop in blood pressure. If chest pain occurs within 24 hours of sildenafil, call 911 and tell the responders.
3. Continue aspirin, atorvastatin and current antihypertensive therapy.
4. Clinic follow-up after a period on nitroglycerin to review symptom frequency.

Cardiology

documents.title: Nitro and the other pill
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Good morning. The heart doctor gave me nitroglycerin tablets last week. It works, the pressure goes away in a couple of minutes, I sit on the stairs when I take it. He said never with the sildenafil from urology within 24 hours. Should I just stop the sildenafil to be safe? I don't want to mix them up. Also do I tell you every time I use the nitro?

documents.title: RE: Nitro and the other pill
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Good questions, Gary.
1. You don't have to stop sildenafil, but the rule is absolute: no nitroglycerin within 24 hours after a sildenafil dose. If you get chest pain during that window, don't take the nitro - call 911 and tell them you took sildenafil. If you'd rather not have to think about it, stopping the sildenafil is a perfectly reasonable choice, and that is up to you.
2. You don't need to message every use, but keep a simple note of how often you need it. If you are needing it more often, it takes more than one tablet, or it comes on with less activity or at rest, call cardiology or us that day.
I've added nitroglycerin to your medication list here. Your cardiology letter came through yesterday.

documents.title: Routine follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
SUBJECTIVE
Routine follow-up. Last cardiology contact was the 10/2024 phone follow-up after the July 2024 visit (positive repeat stress test, nitroglycerin started). He reports no new symptoms: angina only with stairs, same as the past year, relieved by rest or one nitro, no rest pain. Taking metformin, amlodipine, atorvastatin and aspirin every day; nitro and sildenafil as needed and never within a day of each other. Fasting today.

He picked up a flyer in our waiting room for a research study of a new cholesterol-lowering medicine and asks whether he could join and what it involves.

OBJECTIVE
BP 138/86 (scale out of service this morning - no weight today).
Comfortable. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. No edema. Feet unchanged: intact skin, reduced monofilament, diminished pulses.
Fasting labs drawn.

ASSESSMENT / PLAN
1. Interest in clinical trial - We talked through how a trial like this works. Participants are assigned at random, by computer, to the study medicine or a placebo (an inactive pill that looks the same); neither he nor I choose, and usually neither he nor the study staff know which one he is getting until the study ends. That is how the study can tell whether the drug itself works. Taking part is voluntary, he can stop at any time, and his regular care here continues either way. The study team, not us, decides who qualifies. Gave him the study information sheet and coordinator contact from the flyer; he will read it and call them if he wants to go forward.
2. Stable angina - stable pattern; aspirin, atorvastatin, amlodipine, NTG prn. Due for his yearly cardiology visit; gave him their number to book.
3. T2DM with CKD 1 and neuropathy - A1c and BMP today.
4. HTN - amlodipine 5.
5. Hyperlipidemia - lipid panel today; atorvastatin 20.
6. PAD, ED - stable.

RTC 6 months.

Addendum 1/13: A1c 7.2%. Fasting glucose 154. Lipids: TC 210, LDL 130, HDL 45, TG 250. Creatinine 0.8, eGFR 99.

documents.title: January results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hi Gary,
Your fasting labs from Monday: A1c 7.2%, fasting glucose 154. Kidney function normal. Cholesterol: total 210, LDL 130, HDL 45, triglycerides 250 - close to your last few panels.
No changes to your medicines. If you do contact the study team, let me know what they say; I'm happy to send them any records they need with your permission.
